title: How to Track Competitor Offer and Price Changes From Ad Data
excerpt: Turn ad spy data into a pricing and offer watch: what to log each week, how to read discount patterns, and when a rival promotion should change your own plan.
body: Most stores use ad spy tools to borrow creative. That is useful, but the more valuable signal usually sits in the offer itself. The bundle, the discount depth, the free shipping threshold, and the guarantee wording tell you how a competitor is defending margin right now. Track those for a few weeks and you can often see a pricing move coming before it shows up in your own sales numbers.

Set up a simple weekly log. Pick five to ten competitors and record three things for each: the headline offer, the entry price on their hero product, and their shipping threshold. Do not try to capture every ad. You are looking for the offer they keep running, because sustained ads are the ones that are working. One week of logging takes about twenty minutes and gives you a baseline that makes the next month readable.

Read discount patterns as a margin signal rather than a marketing one. A competitor who runs a flat percentage discount every weekend is training customers to wait, which usually means weak full-price conversion. A competitor who bundles instead of discounting is protecting average order value. A competitor who raises the free shipping threshold is quietly pushing shoppers to add one more item. Each of those is a different business, and each calls for a different response.

Watch for changes in the entry product. When a competitor introduces a cheaper starter item or a trial-size version, they are usually trying to lower the acquisition cost of a new customer rather than expand the catalog. That shift matters more than any single ad, because it changes the price band you are competing in at the top of the funnel. Decide deliberately whether to follow, undercut, or move upmarket instead of matching by reflex.

Connect the log to your own calendar. If a rival reliably promotes in the last week of the month, plan your campaign for the week before, when their paid pressure is lower and auction prices are softer. If they go quiet during a supply shortage, that is your window to push. Timing is one of the few advantages a smaller store can build without outspending anyone, and it costs nothing but attention.

Keep the discipline of acting only on repeats. A single discount screenshot is noise. Two consecutive weeks of the same changed offer is a decision, and that is when to adjust pricing, bundles, or shipping thresholds. Log the change, the response you made, and the outcome, so next quarter you are working from evidence instead of memory.
